The uniform-weights Bayes factor under weights the researcher states

Source: R/bf_rescaled.R
bf_rescaled.Rd

A range of shares is not a probability for the counts, so before coding the researcher states how each theory spreads its weight over the shares inside its range. bf_uniform_weights() uses the default, which gives every share in a range the same weight. This function takes the alternative the paper offers, so that a reader who would have weighted the shares differently can see what those weights do to the reported number.

Usage

bf_rescaled(y_W, y_R, a1 = 1, b1 = 1, aR = 1, bR = 1)

Arguments

y_W

Non-negative integer. Count (or summed integer weight) of evidence favorable to the working theory.

y_R

Non-negative integer. Count (or summed integer weight) of evidence favorable to the rival.

a1, b1

Positive numerics. The Beta pair squeezed onto the working theory's range, the shares above one half. Default 1 and 1, the uniform weights.

aR, bR

Positive numerics. The Beta pair squeezed onto the rival's range, the shares at or below one half. Default 1 and 1.

Value

A length-1 numeric: the Bayes factor in favor of the working theory under the stated weights.

Details

The alternative starts from the Beta\((a, b)\) family, a family of distributions for a quantity between zero and one whose two parameters set where the weight piles up: with \(a > b\) toward one, with \(a < b\) toward zero, and with \(a = b\) symmetrically, concentrated in the middle when \(a = b\) is above one and pushed toward both ends when it is below one. Larger values of both parameters concentrate the weight more tightly.

Each theory's range is half as wide as the interval from zero to one, so the researcher squeezes a Beta distribution onto it. If \(X\) has the Beta\((a, b)\) distribution, then \(\theta = 1/2 + X/2\) lies between one half and one, which is the working theory's range, and \(\theta = X/2\) lies between zero and one half, which is the rival's. Squeezing an interval to half its width doubles the density, so the two weighting functions are $$2 f_{a,b}(2\theta - 1) \quad\text{and}\quad 2 f_{a,b}(2\theta),$$ with \(f_{a,b}\) the Beta density. Setting both pairs to \((1, 1)\) gives every share in each range the same weight and returns bf_uniform_weights() exactly.

What the parameters mean substantively

The two pairs are a claim about what each theory predicts, and they move the reported number, so a researcher has to argue for them. At nine observations supporting the working theory against three supporting the rival, the uniform default gives 20.67. Beta(1/2, 1/2) on both sides piles weight at both ends of each range, including right next to one half where the two theories predict nearly the same share, so the counts separate the theories less and the value falls to 9.53. Beta(10, 10) on both sides concentrates each theory near the middle of its range, so the working theory predicts a share near three quarters and the rival a share near one quarter, the two predict more different things, and the value rises to 252.92.

The pairs need not match. A researcher who expects that under either theory the search would still turn up evidence for the other puts both densities next to one half, with a1 = 0.5, b1 = 1 for the working theory and aR = 1, bR = 0.5 for the rival, and gets 7.35 at nine of twelve. A researcher who expects each theory to leave almost no evidence for the other pushes both densities to the far ends, reversing those two pairs, and gets 28.08. The first value is below the paper's threshold of 20 and the second is above it.

Weights on shares are not weights on observations

The weights here are weights on \(\theta\), the share of the evidence supporting the working theory. They are a different object from a weight on an observation, which acts as replication: a document the researcher weights at ten enters as ten observations, and the researcher passes that by summing the weights into y_W and y_R.

See also

bf_uniform_weights() for the uniform default; bf_worst_case(), whose a1, b1 take the same rescaled pair for the working theory's shares while the rival is evaluated at its most favorable share.

Examples

# The uniform default, which is bf_uniform_weights(9, 3).
bf_rescaled(9, 3)
#> [1] 20.67196

# Beta(1/2, 1/2) on both sides: weight next to one half, where the
# two theories claim nearly the same share.
bf_rescaled(9, 3, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)
#> [1] 9.526137

# Beta(10, 10) on both sides: each theory concentrated in the middle
# of its range, so the two claims are far apart.
bf_rescaled(9, 3, 10, 10, 10, 10)
#> [1] 252.9172
